rag.name: SemialgHom
rag.content:
/-- Let `φ : R →+* S` be a ring homomorphism, let `A` be an `R`-algebra and let `B` be
an `S`-algebra. Then `SemialgHom φ A B` or `A →ₛₐ[φ] B` is the ring homomorphisms `ψ : A →+* B`
making lying above `φ` (i.e. such that `ψ (r • a) = φ r • ψ a`).
-/
structure SemialgHom {R S : Type*} [CommSemiring R] [CommSemiring S] (φ : R →+* S)
    (A B : Type*)  [Semiring A] [Semiring B] [Algebra R A] [Algebra S B]
    extends A →ₛₗ[φ] B, RingHom A B

rag.name: SemialgHomClass
rag.content:
class SemialgHomClass (F : Type*) {R S : outParam Type*}
  [CommSemiring R] [CommSemiring S] (φ : outParam (R →+* S)) (A B : outParam Type*)
  [Semiring A] [Semiring B] [Algebra R A] [Algebra S B]
  [FunLike F A B] extends SemilinearMapClass F φ A B, RingHomClass F A B

rag.name: AlgEquivClass.toAlgHomClass
rag.content:
instance (priority := 100) toAlgHomClass (F R A B : Type*) [CommSemiring R] [Semiring A]
    [Semiring B] [Algebra R A] [Algebra R B] [EquivLike F A B] [h : AlgEquivClass F R A B] :
    AlgHomClass F R A B :=
  { h with }

rag.name: AlgEquivClass.toAlgEquiv
rag.content:
/-- Turn an element of a type `F` satisfying `AlgEquivClass F R A B` into an actual `AlgEquiv`.
This is declared as the default coercion from `F` to `A ≃ₐ[R] B`. -/
@[coe]
def toAlgEquiv {F R A B : Type*} [CommSemiring R] [Semiring A] [Semiring B] [Algebra R A]
    [Algebra R B] [EquivLike F A B] [AlgEquivClass F R A B] (f : F) : A ≃ₐ[R] B :=
  { (f : A ≃ B), (f : A ≃+* B) with commutes' := commutes f }

This is declared as the default coercion from `F` to `A ≃ₐ[R] B`. -/
@[coe]
def toAlgEquiv {F R A B : Type*} [CommSemiring R] [Semiring A] [Semiring B] [Algebra R A]
    [Algebra R B] [EquivLike F A B] [AlgEquivClass F R A B] (f : F) : A ≃ₐ[R] B :=
  { (f : A ≃ B), (f : A ≃+* B) with commutes' := commutes f }

rag.name: AlgEquiv.applyMulSemiringAction
rag.content:
/-- The tautological action by `A₁ ≃ₐ[R] A₁` on `A₁`.

This generalizes `Function.End.applyMulAction`. -/
instance applyMulSemiringAction : MulSemiringAction (A₁ ≃ₐ[R] A₁) A₁ where
  smul := (· <| ·)
  smul_zero := map_zero
  smul_add := map_add
  smul_one := map_one
  smul_mul := map_mul
  one_smul _ := rfl
  mul_smul _ _ _ := rfl

instance (priority := 100) toAlgHomClass (F R A B : Type*) [CommSemiring R] [Semiring A]
    [Semiring B] [Algebra R A] [Algebra R B] [EquivLike F A B] [h : AlgEquivClass F R A B] :
    AlgHomClass F R A B :=
  { h with }

informal_statement: For any index set \( I \), commutative semirings \( R \) and \( S \), a family of semirings \( f : I \to \text{Type} \), a semialgebraic homomorphism \( \phi : R \to^* S \), a family of semialgebraic homomorphisms \( g : (i : I) \to A \to^* f(i) \), and an element \( a : A \), the semialgebraic homomorphism \( \text{Pi.semialgHom}\, _\phi g \) applied to \( a \) at index \( i \) equals \( g(i)(a) \). This is a definitional equality.
informal_proof:
The proof is straightforward and follows directly from the definitions involved:
1. **Definition of Pi.semialgHom**: This function takes a family of semialgebraic homomorphisms \( g \) indexed by \( I \) and returns a semialgebraic homomorphism that, when applied to an element \( a \) at index \( i \), simply applies the corresponding homomorphism \( g(i) \) to \( a \).
2. **Reflexivity Proof**: Since the application of \( \text{Pi.semialgHom}\, _\phi g \) to \( a \) at index \( i \) is defined to be \( g(i)(a) \), the equality \( (\text{Pi.semialgHom}\, _\phi g)(a)(i) = g(i)(a) \) holds by definition, with no additional proof required.

id.name: Pi.semialgHom_apply
id.content:
@[simp]
theorem Pi.semialgHom_apply {I : Type*} {R S : Type*} (f : I → Type*) [CommSemiring R] [CommSemiring S]
    (φ : R →+* S) [s : (i : I) → Semiring (f i)] [(i : I) → Algebra S (f i)] {A : Type*}
    [Semiring A] [Algebra R A] (g : (i : I) → A →ₛₐ[φ] f i) (a : A) (i : I) :
  (Pi.semialgHom _ φ g) a i = g i a := rfl

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
